   103→## Feature Deep Dives
   104→
   105→### 1. Self-Hosted IPNS Resolution
   106→
   107→**Current state:** `DelegatedRoutingClient` points at `https://delegated-ipfs.dev/routing/v1`. This is a public good endpoint maintained by the IPFS Foundation, backed by Someguy. It proxies to the Amino DHT and IPNI (cid.contact indexer). Known issues: 502 errors, rate limiting (429), stale records due to caching.
   108→
   109→**Recommendation: Self-host Someguy alongside Kubo.**
   110→
   111→Someguy is the same software powering `delegated-ipfs.dev`. Self-hosting it gives:
   112→- Full control over caching, rate limits, and availability
   113→- Same DHT and IPNI backends, but without shared public infrastructure load
   114→- Docker deployment: `ghcr.io/ipfs/someguy:latest`
   115→- Minimum resources: runs alongside existing Kubo node, shares its DHT participation
   116→- Configuration via environment variables (endpoints, caching, DHT toggles)
   117→
   118→**Architecture:**
   119→```
   120→Client -> CipherBox API -> Self-hosted Someguy -> Amino DHT / IPNI
   121→                        -> DB cache (fallback, sequence-number-aware)
   122→```
   123→
   124→**Fallback chain:**
   125→1. Self-hosted Someguy (primary)
   126→2. DB-cached CID (always fresh for own publishes)
   127→3. delegated-ipfs.dev (emergency fallback, best-effort)
   128→
   129→**Performance expectations (from ProbeLab Week 07, 2026):**
   130→- DHT lookup: 0.3-0.4s median across regions
   131→- Self-hosted avoids public endpoint queuing -- expect lower variance
   132→- Kubo 0.34+ default IPNS TTL: 5 minutes (down from 1 hour) -- faster propagation
   133→
   134→**Complexity:** MEDIUM
   135→- Docker Compose addition for Someguy
   136→- Update `DELEGATED_ROUTING_URL` env var
   137→- Update `DelegatedRoutingClient` for fallback chain
   138→- Scrape Someguy's Prometheus metrics
   139→
   140→**Confidence:** HIGH -- Someguy is the reference implementation for Routing V1. Self-hosting is explicitly documented.
   141→
   142→### 2. Move rootFolderKey to IPFS Vault Record
   143→
   144→**Current state:** `vaults` table stores `encryptedRootFolderKey` (ECIES-wrapped with user's publicKey) and `encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey`. The IPNS private key is deterministically derivable via HKDF, so only `encryptedRootFolderKey` truly needs storage.
   145→
   146→**Recommendation: Embed ECIES-wrapped rootFolderKey in the IPFS blob pointed to by the root vault IPNS record.**
   147→
   148→**New bootstrap flow:**
   149→1. Login with Web3Auth, derive secp256k1 keypair
   150→2. Derive root IPNS private key via HKDF (deterministic, no storage needed)
   151→3. Resolve root IPNS name to get CID
   152→4. Fetch IPFS blob at CID
   153→5. Blob contains: `{ encryptedRootFolderKey: <ECIES>, metadata: <AES-GCM encrypted FolderMetadata> }`
   154→6. Unwrap rootFolderKey with privateKey
   155→7. Decrypt FolderMetadata with rootFolderKey
   156→
   157→**Migration strategy:**
   158→- New blob format versioned (per METADATA_EVOLUTION_PROTOCOL)
   159→- Dual-read period: client checks IPFS blob first, falls back to DB vault record
   160→- Lazy migration: on next folder metadata publish, client writes new-format blob
   161→- After migration period, `vaults.encrypted_root_folder_key` column becomes nullable/deprecated
   162→- Recovery tool updated for new blob format
   163→
   164→**What stays in DB:** `vaults` table retains `owner_id`, `root_ipns_name`, and timestamps. The `owner_public_key` column stays (needed for share ECIES wrapping lookups). Crypto material columns become nullable.
   165→
   166→**Risk:** IPNS resolution failure during login is a hard blocker. Mitigated by:
   167→- DB-cached CID fallback (server stores latest CID in `folder_ipns` table)
   168→- Self-hosted Someguy improving baseline reliability
   169→- Client retries with exponential backoff
   170→
   171→**Complexity:** HIGH
   172→- New IPFS blob envelope format
   173→- Metadata schema version bump
   174→- Migration path (dual-read, lazy migration)
   175→- Recovery tool update
   176→- Desktop app (Rust) must parse new format
   177→- E2E test updates for new login flow
   178→
   179→**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- The approach is sound, but the migration path has edge cases (what if user never logs in during dual-read period? stale recovery tools?).
   180→
   181→### 3. BYO-IPFS Node Support
   182→
   183→**Current state:** `IpfsProvider` interface (`pinFile`, `unpinFile`, `getFile`) with single `LocalProvider` implementation pointing at the server's Kubo instance via env var `IPFS_LOCAL_API_URL`.
   184→
   185→**Recommendation: Add a `RemotePinningProvider` implementing `IpfsProvider` against the IPFS Pinning Service API standard, configured per-user.**
   186→
   187→**The IPFS Pinning Service API** is a vendor-agnostic OpenAPI spec. Endpoints:
   188→- `POST /pins` -- Pin by CID (with origins hint for faster retrieval)
   189→- `GET /pins` -- List pins with filtering
   190→- `GET /pins/{requestid}` -- Status of specific pin
   191→- `DELETE /pins/{requestid}` -- Unpin
   192→- Auth: Bearer token per service
   193→
   194→**Supported services:** Filebase, Pinata (partial -- no IPNS), web3.storage, IPFS Cluster, any self-hosted Kubo with pinning API enabled.
   195→
   196→**Architecture (server-relay mode -- recommended default):**
   197→```
   198→Client -> CipherBox API -> Provider Router -> LocalProvider (default)
   199→                                           -> RemotePinningProvider (user's node)
   200→```
   201→
   202→**Per-user configuration model:**
   203→- New `user_ipfs_config` table or extend vault settings:
   204→  - `pinning_endpoint_url` (e.g., `https://api.filebase.io/v1`)
   205→  - `pinning_auth_token` (encrypted at rest with server key -- or ECIES-wrapped with user's publicKey for zero-knowledge)
   206→  - `provider_type` enum: `default` | `pinning-api` | `kubo-direct`
   207→- Settings UI: endpoint URL, auth token, "test connection" button
   208→
   209→**Key design decisions:**
   210→
   211→1. **Server-relay vs client-direct:** Server-relay because:
   212→   - Quota tracking works (server meters bytes relayed)
   213→   - Conflict detection works (server sees all publishes)
   214→   - No CORS issues
   215→   - User's auth token stored server-side (encrypted)
   216→   - Tradeoff: server sees encrypted blobs transit (acceptable -- data is already encrypted client-side)
   217→
   218→2. **Dual-pin strategy:** Pin to BOTH default node AND user's node. User's node is "additional persistence," not replacement. Ensures CipherBox can still serve the data if user's node goes down.
   219→
   220→3. **IPNS implications:** IPNS publishing still goes through self-hosted Someguy/DHT, not user's node. IPNS is a naming layer, independent of pinning. User's node provides content persistence, not name resolution.
   221→
   222→4. **Quota tracking:** When BYO-IPFS is configured, server-side quota is advisory ("you have X bytes on our node"). User's node quota is user's problem.
   223→
   224→**Complexity:** HIGH
   225→- New provider implementation against Pinning Service API
   226→- Per-user configuration storage
   227→- Provider routing logic (which user gets which provider)
   228→- Settings UI
   229→- "Test connection" flow
   230→- Error handling for unreachable user nodes
   231→- Dual-pin logic
   232→
   233→**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- The Pinning Service API is well-specified, but per-user provider routing in a NestJS DI context needs careful design. Zero-knowledge storage of auth tokens (ECIES-wrapped) adds crypto complexity.
   234→
   235→### 4. Database Minimization (Beyond rootFolderKey)
   236→
   237→**Current DB tables and migration analysis:**
   238→
   239→| Table | Rows Per User | Contains Crypto? | Can Move to IPFS? | Recommendation |
   240→|-------|---------------|------------------|-------------------|----------------|
   241→| `users` | 1 | No | No -- auth identity | KEEP |
   242→| `auth_methods` | 1-5 | No | No -- auth lookup | KEEP |
   243→| `refresh_tokens` | 1-10 | No | No -- session management | KEEP |
   244→| `vaults` | 1 | Yes (`encryptedRootFolderKey`, `encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey`) | Partially -- crypto to IPFS, metadata stays | MIGRATE crypto columns |
   245→| `folder_ipns` | N (folders+files) | Yes (`encryptedIpnsPrivateKey`) | Partially -- CID cache useful, TEE keys needed server-side | KEEP as cache, make optional |
   246→| `pinned_cids` | N (files) | No | Could derive from IPFS pin list | DEFER -- `ipfs pin ls` is slow for large sets |
   247→| `shares` | N (shares) | Yes (`encryptedKey`) | Theoretically via CRDT inbox | KEEP for v1.1, research CRDT for v1.2 |
   248→| `share_keys` | N (per-share) | Yes (`encryptedKey`) | Same as shares | KEEP for v1.1 |
   249→| `share_invites` | N (pending) | Yes | Same as shares | KEEP for v1.1 |
   250→| `ipns_republish_schedule` | N (folders) | No | No -- TEE coordination needs server-side scheduling | KEEP |
   251→
   252→**What realistically moves to IPFS in v1.1:**
   253→1. `vaults.encryptedRootFolderKey` and `vaults.encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey` -> IPFS blob
   254→2. `folder_ipns.latestCid` becomes advisory cache, not authoritative source
   255→3. `folder_ipns.encryptedIpnsPrivateKey` stays -- TEE needs server-accessible copy
   256→
   257→**What stays in DB and why:**
   258→- Auth tables: Indexed lookups required for login flow
   259→- Shares: Complex query patterns (list by recipient, filter by status, revocation state)
   260→- Pinned CIDs: Quota tracking requires fast aggregation queries
   261→- Republish schedule: TEE coordination requires server-side cron state
   262→- Folder IPNS: Sequence numbers needed for conflict detection; CID cache needed for IPNS fallback
   263→
   264→**Realistic v1.1 DB state after migration:**
   265→- Auth-only: `users`, `auth_methods`, `refresh_tokens` (3 tables, no crypto)
   266→- Vault metadata: `vaults` with crypto columns nullable (1 table, crypto migrated)
   267→- IPFS operations: `folder_ipns`, `pinned_cids`, `ipns_republish_schedule` (3 tables, operational cache)
   268→- Sharing: `shares`, `share_keys`, `share_invites` (3 tables, unchanged)
   269→
   270→**Reality check:** The goal of "reduce database to auth-only" is aspirational for v1.1. Realistically, v1.1 can eliminate crypto from `vaults` and make `folder_ipns` an advisory cache. Full share migration requires CRDT research. Full `pinned_cids` elimination requires alternative quota tracking.
   271→
   272→**Complexity:** Per-table varies (see table above). Overall: HIGH for rootFolderKey migration, LOW for making `folder_ipns` advisory, VERY HIGH for share migration (deferred).
   273→
   274→**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- rootFolderKey migration is well-understood. The gap between "auth-only DB" and "realistic v1.1" is significant.

1→# Pitfalls Research
     2→
     3→**Domain:** IPFS infrastructure improvements -- replacing delegated routing, migrating DB state to IPFS/IPNS, BYO-IPFS node support, and performance baselines for an existing zero-knowledge encrypted storage app
     4→**Researched:** 2026-03-07
     5→**Confidence:** HIGH for routing/migration pitfalls (verified against codebase + IPFS docs), MEDIUM for BYO-IPFS (fewer production precedents), MEDIUM for instrumentation (well-understood domain but CipherBox-specific interactions need validation)
     6→
     7→**Context:** CipherBox v1.0 shipped 2026-03-05 with 423K lines of TypeScript + Rust across 698 source files. IPNS is already deeply integrated: the `folder_ipns` table tracks per-folder and per-file IPNS records with sequence numbers for optimistic concurrency, the `ipns_republish_schedule` table drives TEE republishing every 6 hours, and `delegated-ipfs.dev` is the sole external routing provider (known unreliable, with DB-cached CID fallback). The database stores auth, vault keys, shares, device approvals, pinned CIDs for quota tracking, and all IPNS state. The recovery tool (`recovery.html`) directly resolves IPNS via `delegated-ipfs.dev` without any API intermediary.
     8→
     9→---
    10→
    11→## Critical Pitfalls
    12→
    13→Mistakes that cause data loss, break existing functionality, or require rearchitecting completed features.
    14→
    15→---
    16→
    17→### Pitfall 1: Sequence Number Divergence When Switching Routing Providers
    18→
    19→**What goes wrong:**
    20→The system currently has two sources of truth for IPNS sequence numbers: the `folder_ipns` PostgreSQL table and the DHT/delegated routing network. When replacing `delegated-ipfs.dev` with a self-hosted Someguy instance or Kubo DHT, the new routing endpoint may return different sequence numbers than the DB cache for a transition period. The `resolveRecord()` method in `ipns.service.ts` (line 290-350) already compares DB and network sequence numbers, taking the higher one. But during the switch, the new provider may have _no_ records (it has not seen previous publishes), causing resolution to return null from the network while the DB has valid data. If the resolution logic treats "null from network" differently than "null from delegated-ipfs.dev" -- or if the new provider starts returning stale records it picked up from DHT propagation with lower sequence numbers -- the system could serve outdated metadata, causing the client to see old folder contents or triggering false conflict detection (409 Conflict).
    21→
    22→The TEE republishing service (`republish.service.ts`) further complicates this: it publishes signed records to delegated routing and then syncs the sequence number back to `folder_ipns`. If the old and new routing providers are both receiving publishes during a transition window, the sequence number in each may diverge independently.
    23→
    24→**Why it happens:**
    25→- Developers assume a clean cutover is possible -- swap one URL for another
    26→- IPNS records propagate through the DHT with eventual consistency; a new Someguy instance must discover existing records through DHT lookups, which takes time
    27→- The TEE republisher runs on a 6-hour cycle and may publish to the old provider after the API has switched to the new one, creating a split-publish window
    28→
    29→**How to avoid:**
    30→1. Run the new routing provider in read-parallel mode first: configure it alongside `delegated-ipfs.dev` and compare results for at least 48 hours (one full DHT record expiry cycle) before cutting writes over
    31→2. Seed the new provider by having the TEE republisher publish to BOTH providers during the transition. The `publishSignedRecord()` method at line 200-204 sends to one delegated routing client; extend this to dual-write
    32→3. Only cut over reads after the new provider consistently returns sequence numbers >= the DB cache for a representative sample of IPNS names
    33→4. Keep DB cache as the authoritative fallback throughout -- this already works and should remain the primary resolution path
    34→
    35→**Warning signs:**
    36→- IPNS resolve latency spikes or increased null-from-network responses in Prometheus metrics (`cipherbox_ipns_resolves_total` by `source` label)
    37→- 409 Conflict errors on publish that were not present before the switch
    38→- Recovery tool fails to resolve IPNS records (it bypasses the API and hits the routing provider directly)
    39→
    40→**Phase to address:** IPNS Reliability phase (first phase of the milestone)
    41→
    42→---
    43→
    44→### Pitfall 2: Moving rootFolderKey to IPFS Creates a Hard Dependency on IPNS for Login
    45→
    46→**What goes wrong:**
    47→Today, `rootFolderKey` is stored as ECIES-wrapped bytes in the `vaults` table (`encrypted_root_folder_key` column in `vault.entity.ts`). The login flow retrieves it via a direct PostgreSQL query -- fast, reliable, always available. The proposal to move it to an IPFS blob pointed at by the root vault IPNS record means that login now requires: (1) HKDF derivation of IPNS key, (2) IPNS resolution to get the CID, (3) IPFS fetch of the blob, (4) ECIES unwrapping. Steps 2 and 3 are network operations against infrastructure that has documented reliability issues.
    48→
    49→If IPNS resolution fails (which it does -- the entire motivation for this milestone), the user cannot log in because they cannot get their root folder key. The DB-cached CID fallback helps, but it means the database still stores CIDs pointing to encrypted root folder key blobs -- you have not actually eliminated the DB dependency, you have just moved what the DB stores from "ECIES-wrapped key bytes" to "CID of IPFS blob containing ECIES-wrapped key bytes." The net reduction in server-side state is zero unless you also eliminate the CID cache, at which point login depends entirely on IPNS reliability.
    50→
    51→**Why it happens:**
    52→- The goal of "minimize database to auth-only" is laudable but creates a conflict with the reliability requirement
    53→- The rootFolderKey is unique: unlike IPNS private keys which are HKDF-derivable, the root folder key is a random AES-256 key. It literally cannot be rederived. Losing access to it means losing the entire vault.
    54→- Developers see the encryption key as "just data that should live on IPFS" without recognizing it is the single most critical piece of data in the entire system
    55→
    56→**How to avoid:**
    57→1. Keep `encrypted_root_folder_key` in the database as the primary source. Optionally mirror it to IPFS for recovery tool independence, but the DB copy is canonical for login.
    58→2. If the goal is recovery-tool independence from the server, embed the wrapped key in the IPFS vault blob AND keep the DB copy. The recovery tool reads from IPFS; the normal login reads from the DB. Both paths work.
    59→3. Never make the sole access path for root folder key depend on IPNS resolution. This is a "both, not either" situation.
    60→4. Per `METADATA_EVOLUTION_PROTOCOL.md`, this is a breaking change to the root vault blob format. Version the blob format so old clients can still decrypt old-format blobs during migration.
    61→
    62→**Warning signs:**
    63→- Login latency increases from <100ms to multi-second (IPNS resolve is median 11s on DHT per ProbeLab measurements)
    64→- Login failure rate correlates with IPNS availability instead of being independent
    65→- Recovery tool works but normal login fails (or vice versa)
    66→
    67→**Phase to address:** Database Minimization phase -- but this pitfall argues for NOT moving rootFolderKey off the DB at all, or at minimum maintaining a dual-write pattern
    68→
    69→---
    70→
    71→### Pitfall 3: Migrating Shares to IPFS Breaks Recipient-Initiated Discovery
    72→
    73→**What goes wrong:**
    74→The `shares` table enables recipient-initiated share discovery: a recipient calls `GET /shares/received` and the API queries `WHERE recipient_id = :userId`. If shares migrate to IPFS/IPNS (e.g., each user has an "inbox" IPNS record listing shares offered to them), the recipient must now know _where_ to look. In the current model, the server knows; in the IPFS model, either:
    75→
    76→(a) The sharer publishes to the recipient's inbox IPNS record -- but the sharer does not hold the recipient's IPNS private key and cannot sign the record, so this is architecturally impossible without a new key-sharing protocol.
    77→
    78→(b) The sharer publishes to their own IPNS record and the recipient polls all potential sharers -- but the recipient does not know who might share with them.
    79→
    80→(c) A server-side index maps recipients to share IPNS records -- but this puts the discovery mechanism back in the database, negating the migration.
    81→
    82→Additionally, the `share_keys` table stores per-file and per-subfolder ECIES-wrapped keys. Each key is specific to a recipient's public key. These cannot simply be "moved to IPFS" because they reference database UUIDs (`share_id`, `item_id`) for relational joins. The IPFS blob would need to embed all relationship data that currently lives in foreign keys and indices.
    83→
    84→**Why it happens:**
    85→- The mental model "move everything to IPFS" does not account for relational operations like indexed queries on foreign keys
    86→- Share discovery is fundamentally a server-side operation in a system where users cannot enumerate other users' IPNS records
    87→- The existing share-revocation flow uses soft-delete with `revoked_at` timestamp and lazy key rotation -- this stateful lifecycle is hard to model in immutable IPFS blobs
    88→
    89→**How to avoid:**
    90→1. Accept that shares, share_keys, and share_invites are server-side state that SHOULD stay in the database. They are access-control metadata, not user content. The server already sees `sharer_id`, `recipient_id`, and `ipns_name` in plaintext -- moving them to IPFS does not improve privacy.
    91→2. If serverless share discovery is a goal (for BYO-IPFS or full decentralization), research CRDT-based IPNS inbox patterns BEFORE attempting migration. The todo at `2026-02-22-crdt-ipns-inbox-sharing.md` correctly flags this as research-only for this milestone.
    92→3. Categorize DB tables into "can migrate" vs "must stay":
    93→   - **Can migrate:** `folder_ipns` (IPNS tracking), `pinned_cids` (quota tracking if BYO replaces it), vault keys (if dual-written)
    94→   - **Must stay:** `shares`, `share_keys`, `share_invites` (relational discovery), `device_approvals` (cross-device MFA), `users`, `auth_methods`, `refresh_tokens` (auth)
    95→
    96→**Warning signs:**
    97→- Design documents propose "share IPNS records" without specifying how recipients discover them
    98→- The words "poll all sharers" appear in a design doc (quadratic complexity)
    99→- Share acceptance latency goes from instant (DB query) to seconds (IPNS resolution)
   100→
   101→**Phase to address:** Database Minimization phase -- but the actual prevention is to scope "minimize database" more narrowly than "move everything off"
   102→
   103→---
   104→
   105→### Pitfall 4: BYO-IPFS Bypasses Server-Side Optimistic Concurrency
   106→
   107→**What goes wrong:**
   108→CipherBox's conflict detection works because ALL IPNS publishes go through the API, which checks `expectedSequenceNumber` against the `folder_ipns` table before accepting a publish (lines 177-189 of `ipns.service.ts`). When a user configures a BYO-IPFS node and publishes IPNS records directly (client-to-node without API relay), the server never sees the publish and cannot check sequence numbers. Two devices could publish conflicting metadata for the same folder, and the DHT will keep whichever has the higher sequence number -- but neither device knows about the conflict.
   109→
   110→Worse: the TEE republishing service tracks sequence numbers in `ipns_republish_schedule`. If a BYO user publishes directly to their node, the TEE's sequence number becomes stale. The next TEE republish will create a record with a LOWER sequence number than what the user published, causing the DHT to reject it (or worse, a race where different DHT nodes hold different records). The user's IPNS records silently stop being republished.
   111→
   112→**Why it happens:**
   113→- BYO-IPFS is designed for user sovereignty, but the entire concurrency model assumes server mediation
   114→- The provider interface (`IpfsProvider`) only abstracts pin/unpin/fetch -- it does not abstract IPNS publishing, which is handled separately through `DelegatedRoutingClient`
   115→- Client-direct upload to a user's Kubo node is the simplest implementation, but it bypasses every server-side check
   116→
   117→**How to avoid:**
   118→1. Even with BYO-IPFS, require IPNS publishes to go through the API. The server does not need to contact the user's IPFS node for IPNS -- it just needs to see the publish request for concurrency checking and TEE enrollment.
   119→2. Separate the concerns: BYO-IPFS is about WHERE data is pinned, not about HOW metadata is published. Pin encrypted blobs to the user's node; publish IPNS records through the API.
   120→3. If client-direct IPNS publishing is a requirement (full decentralization), implement client-side conflict detection: before publishing, resolve the current IPNS record, compare sequence numbers, and abort on mismatch. This is weaker than server-side checks (no atomicity guarantee) but better than nothing.
   121→4. Add a "last known sequence number" field to the BYO-IPFS configuration so the client can detect when the TEE's sequence diverges from the user's actual sequence.
   122→
   123→**Warning signs:**
   124→- BYO users report "stale" folder contents on other devices
   125→- TEE republish success rate drops for BYO users specifically
   126→- Sequence numbers in `ipns_republish_schedule` are lower than what IPNS resolves to
   127→
   128→**Phase to address:** BYO-IPFS phase -- design decision required before implementation begins
   129→
   130→---
   131→
   132→### Pitfall 5: DHT Record Expiry During Routing Provider Migration
   133→
   134→**What goes wrong:**
   135→IPNS records on the DHT expire after 48 hours regardless of the validity field in the record. Kubo's default republish period is 4 hours, and CipherBox's TEE republishes every 6 hours. During a routing provider migration, if there is a gap where neither the old provider nor the new provider successfully publishes records, the 48-hour expiry clock keeps ticking. If the gap exceeds 48 hours (e.g., a weekend deployment where the new provider is misconfigured), ALL IPNS records for ALL users expire from the DHT simultaneously. Recovery requires republishing every single record -- but the TEE processes records in batches of 100 with a 6-hour cycle, so catching up on thousands of records takes many cycles.
   136→
   137→The DB-cached CID fallback saves resolution, but only for users going through the API. The recovery tool (`recovery.html`) and any future BYO-IPFS clients resolving directly from the DHT will get nothing.
   138→
   139→**Why it happens:**
   140→- The 48-hour DHT expiry is not widely known -- developers assume IPNS records persist until explicitly replaced
   141→- The TEE republish cycle (6 hours) provides comfortable margin (48/6 = 8 missed cycles before expiry), creating false confidence
   142→- Migration testing often happens on small test datasets where a full republish cycle completes quickly, masking the problem at scale
   143→
   144→**How to avoid:**
   145→1. Never take the old routing provider offline until the new one has successfully processed at least one full republish cycle for ALL enrolled records
   146→2. Monitor the `cipherbox_republish_schedule_total` gauge by status during migration -- any spike in `retrying` or `stale` status indicates the new provider is not accepting publishes
   147→3. Before migration, calculate the worst-case catch-up time: `(total enrolled records / BATCH_SIZE) * republish_interval = (N / 100) * 6 hours`. For 1000 records, that is 60 hours to fully catch up from scratch -- already past the 48-hour expiry
   148→4. Consider a one-time "emergency republish" endpoint that processes all records immediately (bypassing the 6-hour schedule) after a provider switch
   149→5. Reduce BATCH_SIZE temporarily during migration to process more records per cycle, or run catch-up cycles more frequently
   150→
   151→**Warning signs:**
   152→- `ipns_republish_schedule` entries accumulating in `retrying` or `stale` status
   153→- IPNS resolution returning null for records that were previously resolvable
   154→- Recovery tool stops working for all users simultaneously
   155→
   156→**Phase to address:** IPNS Reliability phase -- must be addressed in the migration runbook
   157→
   158→---
   159→
   160→### Pitfall 6: Quota Tracking Becomes Unenforceable with BYO-IPFS
   161→
   162→**What goes wrong:**
   163→CipherBox tracks storage quota via the `pinned_cids` table: every upload goes through `IpfsController`, which calls `pinFile()` on the server-managed Kubo node and records the CID + size in `pinned_cids`. The user's total is summed against a 500 MiB limit. With BYO-IPFS, if uploads go directly to the user's node (client-direct), the server never sees the upload and cannot record the CID. The `pinned_cids` table becomes incomplete. Quota enforcement is either (a) impossible, (b) advisory only, or (c) requires the client to self-report, which is trivially forgeable.
   164→
   165→The deeper issue: quota tracking exists to protect the CipherBox operator's IPFS node from unbounded storage consumption. If the user is pinning to their own node, the CipherBox operator has no storage cost and does not need to enforce quota. But the system currently conflates "enforce quota" with "track what the user has stored" -- and that tracking is also used for the recycle bin's CID unpinning (30-day retention + cleanup).
   166→
   167→**Why it happens:**
   168→- The existing quota model assumes all storage flows through the server
   169→- Client-direct upload is the most obvious BYO architecture but breaks server-side bookkeeping
   170→- Developers may add BYO pinning without considering that quota, recycle bin, and orphan cleanup all depend on the `pinned_cids` table
   171→
   172→**How to avoid:**
   173→1. For BYO-IPFS users, skip server-side quota enforcement entirely. The user manages their own node's capacity.
   174→2. Still require BYO uploads to be reported to the API (POST with CID + size after client-side pin succeeds). This maintains the `pinned_cids` ledger for features that depend on it (recycle bin, orphan detection) without requiring the server to handle the actual data.
   175→3. Mark `pinned_cids` entries with a `provider` column ("server" | "byo") so the system knows which CIDs it can directly unpin vs. which require the client to unpin.
   176→4. Accept that unpinning on a BYO node requires client cooperation -- the server cannot reach into the user's node. Document this limitation clearly.
   177→
   178→**Warning signs:**
   179→- BYO users show 0 bytes used in quota display despite having files
   180→- Recycle bin emptying fails silently for BYO-pinned CIDs (unpin calls go to the wrong node)
   181→- Orphan CID detection reports all BYO CIDs as orphans
   182→
   183→**Phase to address:** BYO-IPFS phase

   187→## Technical Debt Patterns
   188→
   189→Shortcuts that seem reasonable but create long-term problems.
   190→
   191→| Shortcut | Immediate Benefit | Long-term Cost | When Acceptable |
   192→|----------|-------------------|----------------|-----------------|
   193→| Dual-write to old and new routing provider "forever" | Safe migration | Double the publish latency, double the failure surface, code complexity of maintaining two routing clients | Only during migration transition; set a hard deadline to remove the old provider within 2 weeks of cutover |
   194→| Skip IPNS signature verification on DB-cached resolutions | Faster resolve, simpler code | DB-cached CIDs are not cryptographically verified -- a compromised DB could serve malicious CIDs | Acceptable only if the DB is trusted infrastructure. The web client at `ipns.service.ts:160-169` already verifies signatures from network resolves but skips it for DB-fallback results |
   195→| BYO users self-report CID sizes for quota | Simple client-direct architecture | Users can lie about sizes; quota is advisory only | Acceptable for tech demonstrator. For production, require server verification of at least one byte-range to confirm size |
   196→| Use DB-cached CID as primary resolution (skip IPNS network entirely) | Instant resolve, no DHT latency | DB becomes single point of truth for metadata location; IPNS becomes decorative | Acceptable as interim step. The current code already prefers DB when it has a newer sequence number. Making this explicit reduces complexity |
   197→| Hardcode Someguy URL instead of making it configurable | Faster initial implementation | Cannot switch providers without code change and redeploy | Never -- use `DELEGATED_ROUTING_URL` env var (already exists in `delegated-routing.client.ts:22-25`). Zero cost to keep it configurable |
   198→| Measure performance baselines during staging only | No production impact | Staging has different latency, load, and network characteristics than production | Never for baselines intended to represent production. Staging baselines are useful only for relative comparison (before/after a change) |

   217→## Performance Traps
   218→
   219→Patterns that work at small scale but fail as usage grows.
   220→
   221→| Trap | Symptoms | Prevention | When It Breaks |
   222→|------|----------|------------|----------------|
   223→| Full DHT resolution on every IPNS resolve | Login takes 11+ seconds (DHT median); folder navigation feels frozen | Use DB-cached CID as primary resolve path; DHT resolve as background refresh (the current code approximates this but still blocks on DHT first) | Immediately -- median 11s latency per ProbeLab measurements on Amino DHT. Already broken for UX |
   224→| TEE republishing all records in sequence | Republish cycle exceeds the 6-hour interval for users with many folders/files; records start expiring before the next cycle | The current BATCH_SIZE=100 with concurrency helps. Monitor `republish_entries_processed_total` vs cycle duration. Add per-user prioritization | At ~600+ enrolled records per cycle (100 batches * 6s avg per batch = 600s = 10 min total, still fine; but network issues or TEE latency can push individual batches to 60s+, at which point 100 batches * 60s = 100 min, approaching limits) |
   225→| Instrumenting every IPFS operation with synchronous logging | Console.log/warn calls on hot paths (the codebase has 50+ console calls per CONCERNS.md) block the event loop; adding structured logging to IPFS pin/unpin adds latency to user-facing uploads | Use async log shipping (not synchronous console). Instrument at the histogram level (timing), not the log level (string formatting). The existing Prometheus setup is the right model |
   226→| Client-side performance measurement using `Date.now()` | Sub-millisecond operations appear as 0ms; timer coarsening in browsers hides real variance | Use `performance.now()` for client-side timing, `process.hrtime.bigint()` for server-side (already used in `http-metrics.interceptor.ts:13`). Set histogram buckets appropriately for the expected range |
   227→| Baseline measurements taken during development with hot caches | Baselines show artificially good numbers because Kubo's blockstore cache, OS page cache, and browser cache are warm | Always include cold-start measurements: restart Kubo, clear browser cache, flush OS page cache. Report both cold and warm baselines |
   228→| BYO-IPFS with user's home node behind NAT | Pin succeeds locally but content is not retrievable by other peers because the node is not reachable. User reports "upload succeeded but file is missing" | Verify content availability after pin by attempting retrieval from a different peer. Warn users about NAT traversal requirements. Kubo's relay/AutoNAT helps but is not guaranteed | Immediately for any user behind consumer NAT (most home connections) |

   232→## Security Mistakes
   233→
   234→Domain-specific security issues beyond general web security, relevant to the IPFS infrastructure changes.
   235→
   236→| Mistake | Risk | Prevention |
   237→|---------|------|------------|
   238→| Exposing Kubo API (port 5001) to BYO users for "direct pinning" | Kubo API has no authentication. Any client with network access can pin/unpin/add content, exhaust disk, or read any pinned content | Never expose Kubo API directly. Use the IPFS Pinning Service API (port-separated, auth-capable) or proxy through the CipherBox API with JWT auth |
   239→| Storing BYO-IPFS node credentials (API tokens, auth headers) in the database without encryption | Server compromise exposes all BYO users' IPFS node credentials | Encrypt BYO config with the user's publicKey (ECIES). Store only the wrapped blob. The client unwraps and uses the credentials client-side |
   240→| Self-hosted Someguy without rate limiting | DoS vector: anyone can flood the delegated routing endpoint with publish/resolve requests, exhausting DHT connections | Deploy Someguy behind a reverse proxy with rate limiting. The existing `delegated-routing.client.ts` handles 429 responses (lines 62-69), so rate-limited responses are gracefully retried |
   241→| Performance baselines that include auth tokens in timing data | Timing side-channels could reveal information about token validation (e.g., shorter response for invalid tokens vs. valid tokens with expired sessions) | Exclude auth endpoints from public-facing performance dashboards. Report only aggregate histograms, not per-request timings. The existing Prometheus setup correctly does this |
   242→| IPNS records signed with leaked TEE epoch keys | If a previous-epoch TEE private key is compromised, an attacker could forge IPNS records for any user whose key was encrypted with that epoch | The 4-week grace period for epoch rotation means old keys are eventually discarded. Ensure the new routing provider validates IPNS record signatures (Someguy does this inherently via the IPNS spec). Monitor for unexpected sequence number regressions |

   260→## "Looks Done But Isn't" Checklist
   261→
   262→Things that appear complete but are missing critical pieces.
   263→
   264→- [ ] **Routing provider replacement:** New provider resolves IPNS names -- but verify it also PUBLISHES reliably. Resolution can fall back to DB; publishing cannot. Test publish + resolve round-trip, not just resolve.
   265→- [ ] **DB-to-IPFS migration for folder_ipns:** folder_ipns rows exist in IPFS blobs -- but verify the TEE republish service still works. It reads `encrypted_ipns_key` and `sequence_number` from the schedule table, not from IPFS. These columns cannot be eliminated if TEE republishing continues.
   266→- [ ] **BYO-IPFS pin integration:** Files pin to user's node -- but verify they are retrievable by the CipherBox API for serving to other devices. Content must be discoverable on the IPFS network, not just locally pinned.
   267→- [ ] **Performance baselines recorded:** Histograms populated in Prometheus -- but verify baselines include error cases. A P99 that excludes 502/504 errors paints a falsely rosy picture.
   268→- [ ] **Recovery tool updated for new routing:** recovery.html points to new routing endpoint -- but verify it works WITHOUT the CipherBox API running. The entire point of the recovery tool is server-independent vault access.
   269→- [ ] **Orphaned IPNS cleanup:** IPNS records migrated off DB -- but verify the orphaned IPNS records from pre-migration are cleaned up. The CONCERNS.md already flags orphaned IPNS records as tech debt.
   270→- [ ] **Sequence number continuity:** After migration, first publish from client succeeds -- but verify the sequence number is correctly incremented from the pre-migration value, not reset to 1. A reset would cause the DHT to prefer the old (higher-sequence) record.
   271→- [ ] **BYO quota display:** Settings page shows BYO config -- but verify the vault storage usage display updates correctly. If `pinned_cids` is incomplete, the UI shows wrong usage.

   275→## Recovery Strategies
   276→
   277→When pitfalls occur despite prevention, how to recover.
   278→
   279→| Pitfall | Recovery Cost | Recovery Steps |
   280→|---------|---------------|----------------|
   281→| Sequence number divergence after provider switch | LOW | DB is authoritative. Force-republish all records from DB state to new provider. Client-side sequence numbers in Zustand stores may be stale -- user must refresh (F5). |
   282→| rootFolderKey inaccessible (IPNS resolution failure) | CRITICAL if DB copy removed; LOW if DB copy retained | If DB copy exists: serve from DB (already the fallback). If DB copy was removed: user must use recovery tool with their private key to re-derive IPNS key, resolve from DHT (may be expired), and fetch from IPFS. If both fail: vault is permanently inaccessible. |
   283→| Shares unreachable after migration to IPFS | HIGH | Must revert to DB-backed shares. If DB tables were dropped: reconstruct from IPFS blobs by scanning each user's share IPNS records, but recipient discovery requires the server index to be rebuilt from scratch. |
   284→| BYO concurrency conflict (two devices wrote different metadata) | MEDIUM | Detect by comparing IPNS records from multiple DHT lookups. The record with the higher sequence number wins. The losing device must fetch the winning metadata and re-apply its changes on top (manual merge). No automated merge exists in the current architecture. |
   285→| 48-hour DHT expiry (all records lost from DHT) | MEDIUM | DB-cached CIDs still work for API-mediated resolution. To restore DHT records: trigger emergency republish of all entries. At BATCH_SIZE=100, 1000 records = 10 batches. If each batch takes 30s, full recovery = 5 minutes for TEE signing + publishing time. |
   286→| Quota tracking broken for BYO users | LOW | Run a reconciliation job: for each BYO user, fetch their folder metadata from IPNS, enumerate all CIDs, check pin status on their node, update `pinned_cids` table. Can be run as a one-time migration or periodic background job. |
   287→| False performance baselines from observer effect | LOW | Re-run baselines with instrumentation disabled, compare. If overhead > 5%, switch to sampling-based measurement (10% sample rate). Document the measurement methodology alongside the baseline numbers. |

    23→## 1. Existing Architecture Summary
    24→
    25→### Current IPNS Flow (What Changes)
    26→
    27→```text
    28→Client                     API                        delegated-ipfs.dev        Kubo
    29→  |                         |                               |                    |
    30→  |-- sign IPNS record ---->|                               |                    |
    31→  |                         |-- upsert folder_ipns (DB) --->|                    |
    32→  |                         |-- PUT /routing/v1/ipns/:name ->|                    |
    33→  |                         |<-- 200 OK or 502 -------------|                    |
    34→  |<-- { sequenceNumber } --|                               |                    |
    35→  |                         |                               |                    |
    36→  |-- resolve IPNS -------->|                               |                    |
    37→  |                         |-- GET /routing/v1/ipns/:name ->|                    |
    38→  |                         |<-- record bytes or 502 --------|                    |
    39→  |                         |-- fallback: query folder_ipns --|                   |
    40→  |<-- { cid, seqNum } -----|                               |                    |
    41→```
    42→
    43→**Key problem:** `delegated-ipfs.dev` is the sole IPNS resolution path from the API. The DB-cached CID is the fallback, but this means the DB is doing double duty as both CID cache and the reliable resolution source. The external service adds latency (10s timeout, 3 retries with backoff) and has documented 502 reliability issues.

    79→## 2. IPNS Resolution: Replace delegated-ipfs.dev
    80→
    81→### 2.1 Recommendation: DB-First Resolution + Kubo DHT Verification
    82→
    83→**Strategy:** Invert the current resolution priority. Make the DB-cached CID the primary resolution source (it is already written synchronously on every publish). Use the self-hosted Kubo node's `/api/v0/name/resolve` endpoint for background DHT verification. Demote `delegated-ipfs.dev` to a disabled-by-default fallback.
    84→
    85→**Why this approach:**
    86→
    87→1. **Eliminates external dependency.** The self-hosted Kubo node already participates in the IPFS DHT. It can resolve IPNS names directly without delegated-ipfs.dev.
    88→2. **DB cache is already the reliable source.** The `IpnsService.resolveRecord()` method (lines 290-350 of `ipns.service.ts`) already prefers DB cache when its sequence number is higher than the network result. Making DB-first explicit simplifies the architecture.
    89→3. **Kubo DHT resolution has improved.** Kubo 0.38+ has sweep providers with 97% fewer DHT lookups for large-scale operations. IPNS TTL defaults dropped from 1 hour to 5 minutes in recent releases, so changes propagate faster.
    90→4. **PubSub for same-node resolution.** Kubo supports `Ipns.UsePubsub` for near-instant IPNS record propagation between connected peers. When both the publishing client and the TEE republisher connect through the same Kubo node, PubSub makes resolution instantaneous.
    91→
    92→### 2.2 Architecture Change
    93→
    94→**Before (current):**
    95→
    96→```text
    97→IpnsService.resolveRecord()
    98→  -> DelegatedRoutingClient.resolve() -> https://delegated-ipfs.dev (primary, 10s timeout)
    99→  -> folder_ipns DB query (fallback on 502/timeout)
   100→  -> Compare sequence numbers, return highest
   101→```
   102→
   103→**After:**
   104→
   105→```text
   106→IpnsService.resolveRecord()
   107→  -> folder_ipns DB query (primary, <5ms)
   108→  -> Return DB result immediately to caller
   109→  -> Async: KuboIpnsClient.resolve() -> http://kubo:5001/api/v0/name/resolve (background)
   110→     -> If DHT has higher sequence number, update DB cache
   111→     -> If DHT fails, no-op (DB is authoritative for our records)
   112→```
   113→

   128→   * POST /api/v0/name/resolve?arg=<ipnsName>&dht-timeout=5s&nocache=true

   161→### 2.4 Publishing Path: Keep Pre-Signed Records for Client Publishes
   162→
   163→The current publishing flow has clients sign IPNS records locally and send pre-signed bytes to the API. This is correct for zero-knowledge -- the server never has the unencrypted IPNS private key. This does NOT change.
   164→
   165→**For client publishes:** The API receives pre-signed record bytes via `POST /ipns/publish`. The API:
   166→1. Upserts the `folder_ipns` DB record (unchanged -- this is the reliable CID source)
   167→2. Broadcasts the pre-signed record to the DHT via Kubo's `/api/v0/routing/put` (replaces delegated-ipfs.dev)
   168→3. Falls back to delegated-ipfs.dev only if Kubo routing put fails and the fallback is enabled
   169→
   170→**For TEE republishes:** The TEE already has the decrypted IPNS private key in hardware. Instead of TEE signing a record and the API broadcasting via delegated routing, the TEE can return the raw Ed25519 private key bytes (still inside the TEE boundary), and the API can:
   171→1. Import the key temporarily into Kubo's keystore (`/api/v0/key/import`)
   172→2. Call `/api/v0/name/publish` directly through Kubo
   173→3. Remove the key from Kubo's keystore (`/api/v0/key/rm`)
   174→
   175→This bypasses delegated-ipfs.dev entirely for republishing. However, this is an optimization, not a requirement. The existing TEE->signed record->delegated routing path still works as a fallback.
   176→
   177→**Security note on Kubo key import:** The IPNS private key is transiently present in Kubo's memory during the publish call. This is acceptable because:
   178→- Kubo already runs on the same host as the API in a Docker network
   179→- The key is encrypted at rest in the DB (encrypted with TEE public key)
   180→- The key is removed from Kubo's keystore immediately after publish
   181→- The alternative (delegated-ipfs.dev) sends the signed record over the internet, which is a larger attack surface
   182→
   183→### 2.5 Kubo Configuration Changes
   184→
   185→Enable on the self-hosted Kubo node:
   186→
   187→```json
   188→{
   189→  "Ipns": {
   190→    "UsePubsub": true
   191→  },
   192→  "Routing": {
   193→    "Type": "auto"
   194→  }
   195→}
   196→```
   197→
   198→`Routing.Type: "auto"` (default) uses both DHT and any configured delegated routers. `Ipns.UsePubsub: true` enables near-instant resolution when both publisher and resolver subscribe to the same pubsub topic. This is especially useful for same-node operations (client publishes, then immediately resolves on the same Kubo instance).

   224→## 3. Database Minimization: Migration Path
   225→
   226→### 3.1 Table-by-Table Analysis
   227→
   228→#### 3.1.1 `vaults.encryptedRootFolderKey` -- MIGRATE TO IPFS
   229→
   230→**Current state:** The `vaults` table stores `encryptedRootFolderKey` (ECIES-wrapped with user's publicKey) and `encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey` (also ECIES-wrapped, but redundant since the IPNS key is HKDF-derivable).
   231→
   232→**Migration:** Move `encryptedRootFolderKey` into the IPFS blob pointed at by the root vault IPNS record. The blob currently contains only AES-GCM encrypted folder metadata. The new format prepends the ECIES-wrapped root folder key.
   233→
   234→**New blob format (version 2):**
   235→
   236→```text
   237→Vault IPFS Blob v2:
   238→  Byte 0:       version = 0x02
   239→  Bytes 1-2:    encryptedRootFolderKey length (uint16, big-endian)
   240→  Bytes 3..N:   ECIES-encrypted rootFolderKey
   241→  Bytes N+1..:  AES-GCM encrypted folder metadata (unchanged)
   242→
   243→Vault IPFS Blob v1 (current, no version byte):
   244→  All bytes:    AES-GCM encrypted folder metadata
   245→```
   246→
   247→Detection: If the first byte is `0x02`, parse as v2. If the first bytes are a valid AES-GCM ciphertext (IV + ciphertext + tag), parse as v1.
   248→
   249→**Login flow change:**
   250→
   251→Before:
   252→```text
   253→Login -> API GET /vault -> { encryptedRootFolderKey, rootIpnsName }
   254→      -> Derive IPNS key via HKDF
   255→      -> Resolve IPNS -> fetch blob -> decrypt metadata with rootFolderKey
   256→```
   257→
   258→After:
   259→```text
   260→Login -> Derive IPNS key via HKDF (no API call needed for key material)
   261→      -> API GET /ipns/resolve?ipnsName=<root> -> { cid }
   262→      -> API GET /ipfs/<cid> -> blob v2
   263→      -> Extract encryptedRootFolderKey from blob header
   264→      -> ECIES decrypt rootFolderKey with privateKey
   265→      -> Decrypt folder metadata with rootFolderKey
   266→```
   267→
   268→**Migration strategy (dual-write, version-aware read):**
   269→
   270→1. **Write path:** Client publishes root metadata in blob v2 format (encryptedRootFolderKey in header). ALSO continues sending encryptedRootFolderKey in the vault init call for backward compatibility with older clients and the current recovery tool.
   271→2. **Read path:** Client checks first byte of blob. v2 -> extract key from blob. v1 or unrecognizable -> fall back to `GET /vault` for the key.
   272→3. **Cutover criteria:** When all active clients support blob v2 reading, the `GET /vault` endpoint can stop returning `encryptedRootFolderKey`. The column is kept in the DB as disaster recovery fallback but is no longer the primary source.
   273→
   274→#### 3.1.2 `vaults.encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey` -- ELIMINATE
   275→
   276→This field is redundant. The root IPNS private key is deterministically derivable from the user's secp256k1 private key via HKDF:
   277→
   278→```text
   279→rootIpnsPrivateKey = HKDF(userPrivateKey, info="cipherbox-root-ipns")
   280→```
   281→
   282→The client already performs this derivation. The server-stored copy was a bootstrapping convenience from v0.1 that is no longer needed. Stop sending it in vault init. Keep the DB column for backward compatibility but mark it deprecated.
   283→
   284→#### 3.1.3 `folder_ipns` -- KEEP BUT REDUCE ROLE
   285→
   286→The `folder_ipns` table currently serves four purposes:
   287→1. **CID cache** -- Reliable fallback when IPNS DHT resolution fails
   288→2. **Sequence number tracking** -- Optimistic concurrency control (409 Conflict detection)
   289→3. **Encrypted IPNS key storage** -- For TEE enrollment
   290→4. **Record type metadata** -- folder vs file distinction
   291→
   292→With reliable Kubo IPNS resolution (section 2):
   293→- Purpose 1 (CID cache) is still valuable as a fast path (<5ms vs seconds for DHT), but no longer critical as the sole reliable source
   294→- Purpose 2 (sequence numbers) is essential and CANNOT move to IPFS. You need to know the current sequence BEFORE publishing. This is inherently a server-side coordination concern.
   295→- Purpose 3 (encrypted IPNS key) is duplicated in `ipns_republish_schedule`. Can be deduplicated by having the republish schedule reference `folder_ipns` instead of storing its own copy. Minor cleanup.
   296→- Purpose 4 (record type) is metadata, could be derived but not worth the effort to remove.
   297→
   298→**Recommendation:** Keep `folder_ipns` as a "publish coordination table." Rename its conceptual role in documentation. Do NOT attempt to eliminate it -- sequence number tracking is a hard requirement for conflict detection.
   299→
   300→#### 3.1.4 `shares`, `share_keys` -- FUTURE (CRDT INBOX RESEARCH ONLY)
   301→
   302→Per the CRDT-based IPNS inbox todo, this milestone performs research only. The tables stay as-is. Key findings:
   303→
   304→- G-Set CRDT solves concurrent share additions (append-only inbox)
   305→- Write-access control via signed envelopes prevents inbox spam
   306→- Revocation by key rotation (not by modifying inbox) aligns with existing lazy revocation pattern
   307→- State size growth needs compaction strategy
   308→- **Dependency:** Requires reliable IPNS resolution (section 2) before inbox-based discovery is viable
   309→- **Scope for v1.1:** Document the CRDT approach as a design RFC. Do NOT implement.
   310→
   311→#### 3.1.5 `device_approvals` -- MIGRATE TO IPFS (POSSIBLE BUT NOT RECOMMENDED)
   312→
   313→Device approvals are short-lived (15-minute expiry), require real-time status updates (pending -> approved/denied), and involve server-mediated notification polling. IPNS polling at 30s intervals is too slow for MFA approval UX. Keep server-side.
   314→
   315→#### 3.1.6 `pinned_cids` -- KEEP (QUOTA ENFORCEMENT)
   316→
   317→The server must enforce storage quotas. If quota tracking moves to IPFS, a malicious client could lie about their storage usage. The server must independently track pinned CID sizes.
   318→
   319→### 3.2 Post-Migration Database Role
   320→
   321→After v1.1 migrations, the database serves these purposes:
   322→
   323→| Purpose | Tables | Why Server-Side |
   324→|---------|--------|-----------------|
   325→| Identity | `users`, `auth_methods` | Server-mediated auth |
   326→| Sessions | `refresh_tokens` | JWT lifecycle |
   327→| Quota enforcement | `pinned_cids` | Server must prevent quota abuse |
   328→| Publish coordination | `folder_ipns` | Sequence numbers for concurrency |
   329→| TEE orchestration | `ipns_republish_schedule`, `tee_key_state`, `tee_key_rotation_log` | Server schedules TEE work |
   330→| Sharing graph | `shares`, `share_keys`, `share_invites` | Until CRDT inbox (v1.2+) |
   331→| MFA | `device_approvals` | Short-lived approval state |
   332→| Vault metadata | `vaults` (reduced) | ownerPublicKey, rootIpnsName only |
   333→
   334→**What was eliminated:** Server no longer stores any user crypto material (encryptedRootFolderKey, encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey). The server becomes a coordination relay, not a key escrow.

   338→## 4. BYO-IPFS Node Support
   339→
   340→### 4.1 Recommendation: Server-Relay Model with Provider Abstraction
   341→
   342→**Decision:** Server-relay (not client-direct) because:
   343→
   344→1. **Quota tracking:** Server must see upload sizes to enforce quota. Client-direct bypasses quota enforcement entirely.
   345→2. **IPNS publish coordination:** Sequence numbers are tracked server-side in `folder_ipns`. Bypassing the API means no conflict detection.
   346→3. **CORS/connectivity:** Kubo's RPC API has no CORS headers by default. Client-direct from the browser requires the user's node to be publicly accessible or configured with CORS -- unreliable for home nodes behind NAT.
   347→4. **Credential safety:** Server-relay means user's IPFS node credentials (API keys, auth tokens) are stored server-side, but the data passing through is already AES-256-GCM encrypted ciphertext. The server cannot read content regardless of relay model.
   348→
   349→**Future exception:** Desktop clients (Tauri) can pin directly to a user's local Kubo node because there are no CORS restrictions and the desktop app is trusted. This is a v1.2+ enhancement.
   350→
   351→### 4.2 Provider Abstraction Extension
   352→
   353→Extend the existing `IpfsProvider` with a per-user factory:
   354→
   355→```typescript
   356→// apps/api/src/ipfs/providers/ipfs-provider.interface.ts -- ADDITIONS
   357→export interface IpfsProviderFactory {
   358→  /** Get the appropriate IPFS provider for a given user */
   359→  getProvider(userId: string): Promise<IpfsProvider>;
   360→  /** Get the default (CipherBox-managed) provider */
   361→  getDefaultProvider(): IpfsProvider;
   362→}
   363→
   364→export const IPFS_PROVIDER_FACTORY = 'IPFS_PROVIDER_FACTORY';
   365→```
   366→
   367→The factory checks for per-user IPFS configuration. If none exists, it returns the default `LocalProvider`. If the user has a custom node configured, it returns a dual-pin provider that pins to both nodes.
   368→
   369→### 4.3 New Provider: UserCustomProvider
   370→
   371→```typescript
   372→// apps/api/src/ipfs/providers/user-custom.provider.ts
   373→export class UserCustomProvider implements IpfsProvider {
   374→  constructor(
   375→    private readonly endpoint: string,
   376→    private readonly authToken?: string,
   377→    private readonly providerType: 'kubo' | 'pinning-api',
   378→  ) {}
   379→
   380→  async pinFile(data: Buffer): Promise<{ cid: string; size: number }> {

   382→      // Kubo RPC: POST /api/v0/add?pin=true&cid-version=1

   384→    } else {
   385→      // IPFS Pinning Service API (spec: ipfs.github.io/pinning-services-api-spec)
   386→      // POST /pins with CID (requires content already available on IPFS network)
   387→      // For fresh uploads, use /api/v0/add equivalent or add+pin flow
   388→      return this.pinViaPinningApi(data);
   389→    }
   390→  }

   392→  async unpinFile(cid: string): Promise<void> { /* provider-specific unpin */ }

   398→
   399→| Provider Type | Protocol | Examples | Auth Method |

400→|--------------|----------|----------|-------------|

   404→### 4.4 Dual-Pin Provider
   405→
   406→The actual provider used for BYO-IPFS users wraps both the default and custom providers:
   407→
   408→```typescript
   409→// apps/api/src/ipfs/providers/dual-pin.provider.ts
   410→export class DualPinProvider implements IpfsProvider {
   411→  constructor(
   412→    private readonly defaultProvider: IpfsProvider,
   413→    private readonly customProvider: IpfsProvider,
   414→  ) {}
   415→
   416→  async pinFile(data: Buffer): Promise<{ cid: string; size: number }> {
   417→    // Always pin to default (CipherBox) node first -- this is the reliable source
   418→    const result = await this.defaultProvider.pinFile(data);
   419→
   420→    // Best-effort pin to user's custom node
   421→    try {
   422→      await this.customProvider.pinFile(data);
   423→    } catch (error) {
   424→      // Log warning but do NOT fail the upload
   425→      logger.warn(`BYO-IPFS pin failed: ${error.message}`);
   426→    }
   427→
   428→    return result; // Return CID from default node
   429→  }
   430→
   431→  async getFile(cid: string): Promise<Buffer> {
   432→    // Try default node first, fall back to custom
   433→    try {
   434→      return await this.defaultProvider.getFile(cid);
   435→    } catch {
   436→      return await this.customProvider.getFile(cid);
   437→    }
   438→  }
   439→
   440→  async unpinFile(cid: string): Promise<void> {
   441→    // Only unpin from CipherBox's node (user manages their own retention)
   442→    await this.defaultProvider.unpinFile(cid);
   443→  }
   444→}
   445→```

   451→  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),

   453→  provider_type VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'default',  -- 'default' | 'kubo' | 'pinning-api'
   454→  endpoint_url VARCHAR(500),
   455→  auth_token_encrypted BYTEA,                             -- encrypted with server-side key
   456→  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
   457→  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
   458→);
   459→```
   460→
   461→**`auth_token_encrypted`:** Encrypted with a server-side symmetric key (from env var), NOT the user's key. The server needs to decrypt it to authenticate with the user's IPFS node. This is acceptable because the data being relayed is already AES-256-GCM encrypted ciphertext -- the server cannot read it regardless.

   488→### 4.8 IPNS and Conflict Detection Implications
   489→
   490→BYO-IPFS affects ONLY where encrypted data is pinned. It does NOT affect:
   491→
   492→- **IPNS publishing:** All publishes still go through the CipherBox API. The client signs IPNS records, the API broadcasts to the DHT.
   493→- **Sequence numbers:** Still tracked in `folder_ipns`. Conflict detection is unchanged.
   494→- **TEE republishing:** Unaffected -- TEE uses CipherBox's Kubo node.
   495→- **IPNS resolution:** Unaffected -- IPNS resolves to a CID, and the CID is available from any node that has it pinned.
   496→
   497→If a future version allows publishing directly to the user's node (bypassing the API), conflict detection would need to move client-side. This is NOT in v1.1 scope.

   726→## 7. Data Flow Changes
   727→
   728→### 7.1 IPNS Resolution (Changed)
   729→
   730→**Before:**
   731→```text
   732→Client -> API /ipns/resolve
   733→  -> DelegatedRoutingClient.resolve() [10s timeout, 3 retries]
   734→  -> Parse IPNS record bytes
   735→  -> Compare with DB-cached CID (folder_ipns)
   736→  -> Return highest sequence number result
   737→```
   738→
   739→**After:**
   740→```text
   741→Client -> API /ipns/resolve
   742→  -> DB query folder_ipns WHERE ipnsName = ? [<5ms]
   743→  -> Return DB result immediately
   744→  -> Fire-and-forget: KuboIpnsClient.resolve() [5s DHT timeout]
   745→    -> If DHT has higher sequence number, update folder_ipns
   746→    -> If DHT fails, no-op
   747→```
   748→
   749→### 7.2 IPNS Publishing (Changed for TEE Path)
   750→
   751→**Before (TEE republish):**
   752→```text
   753→RepublishService -> TeeService.republish() -> signed record bytes
   754→                 -> DelegatedRoutingClient.publish() -> delegated-ipfs.dev
   755→```
   756→
   757→**After (TEE republish, preferred path):**
   758→```text
   759→RepublishService -> TeeService.republish() -> signed record bytes
   760→                 -> KuboIpnsClient.importKey() -> Kubo keystore
   761→                 -> KuboIpnsClient.publish() -> Kubo DHT native
   762→                 -> KuboIpnsClient.removeKey() -> cleanup
   763→                 -> Fallback: DelegatedRoutingClient.publish() if Kubo fails
   764→```
   765→
   766→### 7.3 Vault Access on Login (Changed)
   767→
   768→**Before:**
   769→```text
   770→Client -> API GET /vault -> { encryptedRootFolderKey, rootIpnsName, teeKeys }
   771→       -> Derive IPNS key via HKDF
   772→       -> API GET /ipns/resolve -> { cid }
   773→       -> API GET /ipfs/<cid> -> blob v1 (encrypted metadata only)
   774→       -> Decrypt metadata with rootFolderKey from vault response
   775→```
   776→
   777→**After (v1.1, with blob v2):**
   778→```text
   779→Client -> API GET /vault -> { rootIpnsName, teeKeys, ownerPublicKey }
   780→       -> Derive IPNS key via HKDF
   781→       -> API GET /ipns/resolve -> { cid }
   782→       -> API GET /ipfs/<cid> -> blob v2
   783→       -> Parse blob: extract encryptedRootFolderKey header
   784→       -> ECIES decrypt rootFolderKey with privateKey
   785→       -> Decrypt metadata with rootFolderKey
   786→       -> Fallback: if blob is v1, GET /vault.encryptedRootFolderKey
   787→```
   788→
   789→### 7.4 BYO-IPFS Upload (New)
   790→
   791→```text
   792→Client -> encrypt file -> API POST /ipfs/upload { file }
   793→       -> ProviderFactory.getProvider(userId)
   794→       -> If user has custom config:
   795→         -> DualPinProvider.pinFile(data)
   796→           -> LocalProvider.pinFile(data)           // CipherBox node (always, reliable)
   797→           -> UserCustomProvider.pinFile(data)       // User node (best-effort, logged)
   798→       -> If no custom config:
   799→         -> LocalProvider.pinFile(data)             // CipherBox node only

800→       -> VaultService.recordPin(userId, cid, size) // Quota tracking (unchanged)
   801→       -> return { cid, size }
   802→```
   803→
   804→### 7.5 BYO-IPFS Download (New Path)
   805→
   806→```text
   807→Client -> API GET /ipfs/:cid
   808→       -> ProviderFactory.getProvider(userId)
   809→       -> If user has custom config:
   810→         -> DualPinProvider.getFile(cid)
   811→           -> Try LocalProvider.getFile(cid)         // CipherBox node first
   812→           -> If not found: UserCustomProvider.getFile(cid)  // Fall back to user node
   813→       -> If no custom config:
   814→         -> LocalProvider.getFile(cid)
   815→       -> return file buffer
   816→```

   820→## 8. Suggested Build Order
   821→
   822→### Phase 1: Performance Instrumentation
   823→
   824→**Why first:** Zero risk to existing functionality. Purely additive. Establishes baselines BEFORE making any architectural changes. Without baselines, we cannot measure whether subsequent phases improve or regress performance.
   825→
   826→**Scope:**
   827→- Add 4 new Prometheus histograms to `MetricsService`
   828→- Instrument `IpnsService.resolveRecord()` and `publishRecord()` with timing
   829→- Instrument `IpfsController` upload/download/unpin with timing
   830→- Instrument `RepublishService.processRepublishBatch()` with timing
   831→- Create client-side `perf.ts` utility
   832→- Instrument key web app operations (folder navigate, upload, download)
   833→- Run standardized baseline collection against staging
   834→- Document baselines in `.planning/baselines/`
   835→
   836→**Dependencies:** None. Uses existing `prom-client` and `MetricsService` infrastructure.
   837→**Risk:** LOW. Additive instrumentation only. No behavioral changes.
   838→**Estimated scope:** Small. ~10 modified files, no new entities or migrations.
   839→
   840→### Phase 2: IPNS Resolution Improvement
   841→
   842→**Why second:** Fixes the most critical reliability issue (delegated-ipfs.dev dependency). Required before Phase 3 because moving rootFolderKey to IPFS makes IPNS resolution a login-critical path. Baselines from Phase 1 enable before/after comparison.
   843→
   844→**Scope:**
   845→- Implement `KuboIpnsClient` for native Kubo IPNS resolution
   846→- Refactor `IpnsService.resolveRecord()` to DB-first with async DHT verification
   847→- Make `DelegatedRoutingClient` optional with config flag (`IPNS_DELEGATED_ROUTING_ENABLED`)
   848→- Configure Kubo with `Ipns.UsePubsub: true`
   849→- Optionally update `RepublishService` to use Kubo native publish
   850→- Update recovery tool IPNS resolution fallback chain
   851→- Measure resolution latency against Phase 1 baselines
   852→
   853→**Dependencies:** Phase 1 (for before/after measurement).
   854→**Risk:** MEDIUM. Changing the resolution path could cause resolution failures if Kubo DHT is slower than expected. Mitigated by: (1) DB-first strategy means the fast path is always local, (2) delegated routing remains as a disabled-by-default fallback, (3) existing retry logic in the delegated client.
   855→**Estimated scope:** Medium. 1 new file, ~5 modified files, Kubo config change.
   856→
   857→### Phase 3: Database Minimization (rootFolderKey to IPFS)
   858→
   859→**Why third:** Requires reliable IPNS resolution (Phase 2). The vault blob v2 format is a breaking metadata change that needs careful migration across web, desktop, and recovery tool.
   860→
   861→**Scope:**
   862→- Define vault blob v2 format in `packages/crypto/src/vault/`
   863→- Implement blob v2 serialization/deserialization
   864→- Implement dual-write in web client (blob v2 on publish, DB on vault init)
   865→- Implement version-aware blob reading (v2 -> extract key, v1 -> fall back to DB)
   866→- Update vault init flow to make encryptedRootFolderKey optional
   867→- Mark encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey as deprecated
   868→- Update recovery tool for blob v2 format
   869→- Update desktop client blob parsing
   870→- Migration testing: new user, existing user upgrade, recovery
   871→- Update `docs/METADATA_SCHEMAS.md` per evolution protocol
   872→
   873→**Dependencies:** Phase 2 (IPNS must be reliable before making it login-critical).
   874→**Risk:** MEDIUM-HIGH. Metadata format change affects all clients. Mitigated by: (1) dual-write ensures backward compatibility, (2) version detection allows graceful fallback, (3) DB column is never dropped -- kept as disaster recovery.
   875→**Estimated scope:** Large. New type definitions, serialization code, changes in 3 clients (web, desktop, recovery).
   876→
   877→### Phase 4: BYO-IPFS Node Support
   878→
   879→**Why last:** Largest surface area (new entity, new providers, new UI, new API endpoints). Benefits from stable IPNS resolution (Phase 2) and reduced DB dependency (Phase 3). Independent in design but benefits from the improved infrastructure.
   880→
   881→**Scope:**
   882→- Create `user_ipfs_config` entity and migration
   883→- Implement `UserCustomProvider` with Kubo RPC and Pinning Service API support
   884→- Implement `DualPinProvider` wrapper
   885→- Implement `ProviderFactory` for per-user provider resolution
   886→- Refactor `IpfsController` to use factory
   887→- Add IPFS config CRUD endpoints to vault controller
   888→- Add connection test endpoint
   889→- Build IPFS node configuration UI in settings page
   890→- Implement dual-pin strategy (CipherBox node always + user node best-effort)
   891→- Add BYO-IPFS specific Prometheus metrics
   892→- E2E test: configure custom node, upload, verify pinned
   893→
   894→**Dependencies:** Phase 2 (reliable IPNS) and Phase 3 (reduced DB) are not strict blockers but provide a better foundation.
   895→**Risk:** MEDIUM. New provider implementations need thorough testing against real IPFS nodes and pinning services. Connectivity to arbitrary user nodes introduces unpredictable failure modes. Mitigated by: (1) dual-pin always keeps a copy on CipherBox node, (2) best-effort approach for user node, (3) connection test endpoint validates before saving config.
   896→**Estimated scope:** Large. New entity, migration, 4+ new files, UI component, multiple API endpoints.
   897→
   898→### Build Order Summary
   899→
   900→```text
   901→Phase 1: Performance Instrumentation
   902→    [No dependencies, zero-risk baseline establishment]
   903→    |
   904→    v
   905→Phase 2: IPNS Resolution Improvement
   906→    [Eliminates delegated-ipfs.dev, enables Phase 3]
   907→    |
   908→    v
   909→Phase 3: Database Minimization
   910→    [Moves rootFolderKey to IPFS, requires reliable IPNS from Phase 2]

   918→
   919→**Parallel opportunity:** Phase 4's design and provider implementation can be developed in parallel with Phase 3's blob format work, but integration testing should wait for Phase 3 completion.
